--- title: "Predictive Regression" description: "Chapter 13: measuring prediction error, overfitting with many predictors, ridge, lasso, and elastic net, boosting with Gradient Boosting, model comparison, and the final test." format: deck-html execute: echo: false freeze: auto --- # Predictive Regression Many predictors, few cases, and a number to predict **Chapter 13** Polla Fattah --- ## By the end of today you can - measure numeric predictions with RMSE, MAE, and R², against a baseline; - explain why ordinary regression overfits with many predictors; - fit and tune ridge, lasso, and elastic net regression; - read which predictors the lasso keeps, and what that does not mean; - explain how boosting builds a model from small trees, and tune Gradient Boosting; - choose a model by cross-validation, and report the final test. --- ## Many predictors, few cases A questionnaire, several rounds of measurement, and a background survey can supply 50 predictors for 60 people. Ordinary regression estimates a coefficient for each, fits its own data almost perfectly, and predicts new cases badly. Correlated predictors, like questionnaire items, make it worse. --- ## The question: final GPA from year one The university's advisers meet students at the end of year one. | May use | May not use | |---|---| | background | anything after year one | | all 22 questionnaire items | the workshop's later effects | | semester 1 and 2 records | | The outcome, GPA in semester 4, is a number: a **regression** problem. --- ## One row per student, wide ```python year_one = s12.pivot( index='student_id', columns='semester', values=['gpa', 'sleep_hours', 'study_hours', 'exercise_days', 'caffeine_mg', 'supervisor_meetings', 'wellbeing'] ) year_one.columns = [f"{col[0]}_s{col[1]}" for col in year_one.columns] ``` Column names become `gpa_s1`, `gpa_s2`, `sleep_hours_s1`, etc. --- ## Only students who stayed have a final GPA ```python gpa_data = ( students .merge(questionnaire, on='student_id') .merge(year_one, on='student_id') .merge(final_gpa, on='student_id') .drop(columns=['student_id', 'supervisor_id', 'considering_dropout']) ) ``` `merge(final_gpa, on='student_id')` keeps students with a final GPA: 37 students who left are excluded. The model predicts only for students who stay, and must not be used to judge the leavers. --- ## Split, folds, and recipe ```python X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split( X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=2026 ) gpa_folds = KFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=2026) gpa_recipe = ColumnTransformer([ ('num', Pipeline([ ('impute', SimpleImputer(strategy='median')), ('scale', StandardScaler()) ]), numeric_cols), ('cat', Pipeline([ ('impute', SimpleImputer(strategy='most_frequent')), ('dummy', OneHotEncoder(drop='first', sparse_output=False, handle_unknown='ignore')) ]), categorical_cols) ]) ``` After one-hot encoding categorical variables: 51 predictors. --- ## Errors of a numeric prediction | Actual | Predicted | Error | |---|---|---| | 3.2 | 3.0 | 0.2 | | 2.8 | 2.9 | −0.1 | | 3.6 | 3.3 | 0.3 | | 3.0 | 3.1 | −0.1 | | 2.5 | 2.9 | −0.4 | Each **error** is actual minus predicted ($y - \hat{y}$). --- ## Three summaries of the errors | Measure | Definition | Here | |---|---|---| | MAE | average size of the errors ($\frac{1}{n}\sum |y - \hat{y}|$) | 0.22 | | RMSE | square root of average squared error ($\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum (y - \hat{y})^2}$) | larger; punishes big misses | | R² | variance explained ($1 - \frac{SS_{\text{res}}}{SS_{\text{tot}}}$) | share captured, 0 to 1 | ```python from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error, mean_absolute_error, r2_score ``` MAE and RMSE are in GPA points, lower is better: "typically off by about 0.2". --- ## Always compare with a baseline ```python null_pipe = Pipeline([ ('prep', gpa_recipe), ('model', DummyRegressor(strategy='mean')) ]) ``` Predict the training mean for everyone: RMSE 0\.32. Any useful model must do clearly better. --- ## Ordinary regression with every predictor ```python lm_pipe = Pipeline([ ('prep', gpa_recipe), ('model', LinearRegression()) ]) ``` Cross-validated RMSE 0\.220: much better than the baseline. With 422 students and 51 predictors, it works reasonably. Theses often have 60. --- ## The same model on 60 students ```python lm_small = Pipeline([('prep', gpa_recipe), ('model', LinearRegression())]).fit(X_small, y_small) ``` | Evaluated on | RMSE | |---|---| | its own 60 students | 0\.09 | | new students | 0\.60 | | baseline (the mean) | 0\.32 | Excellent on its own data, worse than predicting the average on new data. --- ## Multicollinearity Six stress items, two semesters of GPA: many predictors are strongly correlated. Regression struggles to divide credit between them. Coefficients become large, unstable, even of opposite signs, cancelling out on training data but not on new data. --- ## Regularisation penalises large coefficients $$ \text{sum of squared errors} + \alpha \times \text{size of coefficients} $$ | Penalty $\alpha$ | Effect | |---|---| | 0 | ordinary regression | | larger | coefficients **shrunk** towards zero | A little shrinkage costs almost no training fit and buys substantial stability. Predictors must be standardised. --- ## Ridge, lasso, and elastic net | Method | Penalty | Effect | |---|---|---| | ridge | $\sum \beta_j^2$ ($L_2$) | shrinks all; keeps every predictor | | lasso | $\sum |\beta_j|$ ($L_1$) | shrinks, and sets some to exactly zero | | elastic net | $\rho \sum |\beta_j| + (1-\rho) \sum \beta_j^2$ | balance between ridge and lasso | In scikit-learn: `Ridge(alpha=...)`, `Lasso(alpha=...)`, `ElasticNet(alpha=..., l1_ratio=...)`. --- ## A lasso on the same 60 students ```python lasso_small = Pipeline([ ('prep', gpa_recipe), ('model', Lasso(alpha=0.03, random_state=2026)) ]).fit(X_small, y_small) ``` | Model on 60 students | RMSE on new students | |---|---| | ordinary regression | 0\.60 | | lasso | 0\.22 | The penalty kept the model from chasing noise. --- ## Shrinkage, coefficient by coefficient ::: {#a9dba2c5 .cell fig-height='3.8' fig-width='7' execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](13-predictive-regression_files/figure-html/cell-3-output-1.png){width=654 height=347} ::: ::: The lasso keeps 11 of 51 predictors and shrinks even those. --- ## Coefficients that make no sense | Predictor | Ordinary regression | Lasso | |---|---|---| | semester 1 GPA | 0\.22 | 0\.09 | | semester 2 GPA | 0\.02 | 0\.11 | | semester 2 caffeine | \-0\.16 | 0\.00 | With 60 students, ordinary regression fits chance patterns. Shrunken coefficients cannot chase one sample's noise. --- ## Tuning penalty $\alpha$ ```python alphas = np.logspace(-4, 0, 20) lasso_grid = GridSearchCV( Pipeline([('prep', gpa_recipe), ('model', Lasso(random_state=2026, max_iter=5000))]), param_grid={'model__alpha': alphas}, cv=gpa_folds, scoring='neg_root_mean_squared_error' ).fit(X_train, y_train) ``` 20 penalties on a log scale, for ridge, elastic net, and lasso. --- ## Too little, just right, too much ::: {#b380ab19 .cell fig-height='3.6' fig-width='8' execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](13-predictive-regression_files/figure-html/cell-4-output-1.png){width=750 height=327} ::: ::: At the far right, lasso zeros every coefficient: back to baseline. Best: $\alpha \approx$ 0\.013. --- ## What the lasso keeps ```python best_lasso = lasso_grid.best_estimator_ best_coefs = best_lasso.named_steps['model'].coef_ ``` Of 51 predictors, the lasso keeps 9. Year-one GPA dominates. One SD higher semester 2 GPA: about 0\.15 points higher final GPA. --- ## The lasso path ::: {#66b78030 .cell fig-height='3.6' fig-width='8' execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](13-predictive-regression_files/figure-html/cell-5-output-1.png){width=750 height=327} ::: ::: As the penalty falls, predictors enter one by one. The two GPA measures enter first. --- ## Selected is not the same as causal Sleep affects GPA (Chapter 8), yet the lasso drops it. Its effect is already visible in year-one GPA, so it adds little to the **prediction**. Among correlated predictors the lasso keeps one, and which one can change between samples. Predict with the lasso; explain with Chapters 8 and 10. --- ## Boosting ```{mermaid} flowchart LR A["Start:
the average"] --> B["Fit a small tree
to the errors"] --> C["Add it,
scaled down"] C -->|repeat hundreds of times| B ``` Each tree learns what the model so far missed. The **learning rate** keeps each step small. Many weak trees add up to a strong model. --- ## Boosting with one predictor ::: {#acfbc7fb .cell fig-height='3.4' fig-width='9' execution_count=5} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](13-predictive-regression_files/figure-html/cell-6-output-1.png){width=846 height=308} ::: ::: One step, a staircase, then a curve that follows the data. --- ## Forests and boosting | | Random forest | Boosting | |---|---|---| | trees grown | independently | in sequence | | combined by | averaging | adding corrections | | main settings | trees, `max_features` | trees, `learning_rate`, `max_depth` | `GradientBoostingRegressor` fits trees sequentially to correct the ensemble's residual errors. --- ## Tuning Gradient Boosting ```python gb_grid = GridSearchCV( Pipeline([('prep', gpa_recipe), ('model', GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=500, random_state=2026))]), param_grid={'model__learning_rate': [0.01, 0.03, 0.1], 'model__max_depth': [1, 2, 4]}, cv=gpa_folds, scoring='neg_root_mean_squared_error' ).fit(X_train, y_train) ``` Best: depth 1, RMSE 0\.211. Depth-1 trees add separate effects with no interactions. Shallow winning means few interactions to find. --- ## Comparing the models ::: {#2f493241 .cell execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}
Model CV RMSE Std. Error
0 lasso 0.204 0.008
1 elastic net 0.204 0.008
2 Gradient Boosting 0.211 0.009
3 ridge 0.220 0.009
4 linear regression 0.220 0.009
5 baseline (mean) 0.322 0.010
``` ::: ::: Lasso and elastic net on top, Gradient Boosting and ridge close behind, all better than ordinary regression. The lasso is chosen for using only 9 predictors. --- ## The final test ```python y_pred_test = final_lasso_model.predict(X_test) ``` | MAE | RMSE | R² | |---|---|---| | 0\.16 | 0\.19 | 0\.66 | Off by 0\.16 GPA points on average, capturing 66% of the variation. --- ## Predicted against actual ::: {#3d10220c .cell fig-height='4' fig-width='5' execution_count=7} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](13-predictive-regression_files/figure-html/cell-8-output-1.png){width=376 height=366} ::: ::: Predictions are less spread than reality: extreme students are pulled towards the average. --- ## How much does year one add to past grades? ```python gpa_only_pipe = Pipeline([ ('impute', SimpleImputer(strategy='mean')), ('model', LinearRegression()) ]).fit(X_train[['gpa_s1', 'gpa_s2']], y_train) ``` | Model | Test RMSE | |---|---| | lasso with everything | 0\.192 | | two year-one GPAs only | 0\.191 | Past grades are by far the best predictor. Sleep, stress, and support matter (Chapter 8), but their influence is already in the grades. --- ## In your field: engineering ```python c_lm = LinearRegression().fit(cX_train, cy_train) c_gb = GradientBoostingRegressor( n_estimators=500, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=4, random_state=1 ).fit(cX_train, cy_train) ``` Concrete strength from its recipe and age: curves and interactions. Boosting cuts RMSE from 10\.90 to 4\.55 MPa. Flexible models win when the data has structure for them. --- ## Practical lab: the Chapter 13 playground Work through the playground exercises in your browser, with hints and solutions. The browser version uses Pyodide to run scikit-learn, NumPy, and pandas right in your browser. --- ## Practical exercises 1–3: errors and shrinkage 1. MAE and RMSE by hand; change one prediction by 1.0 and compare. 2. Repeat the 60-student experiment with 150 students. 3. Ridge against lasso coefficients: how many are exactly zero? --- ## Practical exercises 4–6: design and communication 4. Scale scores instead of 22 items: does the lasso's RMSE change? 5. Gradient Boosting with 100, 500, and 1000 trees at learning rate 0.03. 6. Explain an RMSE of 0.2 to academic advisers in two sentences. --- ## Try this yourself Take a prediction problem from your own field: - count your cases and your predictors; - name a baseline prediction; - decide whether a lasso, a ridge, or boosting suits the structure; - plan how you would report the final test. --- ## Troubleshooting guide (Part 1) | Symptom | Likely cause | |---|---| | near-perfect training fit, poor new predictions | too many predictors for the cases | | coefficients huge and of opposite signs | multicollinearity | | regularisation changes nothing | predictors not standardised | | the lasso predicts the mean for everyone | penalty $\alpha$ too large | --- ## Troubleshooting guide (Part 2) | Symptom | Likely cause | |---|---| | a different lasso selection each sample | correlated predictors; selection is unstable | | the lasso "drops" a known cause | its effect is carried by another predictor | | RMSE reported without a baseline | the number cannot be judged | | extremes predicted too close to the mean | normal for imperfect models | --- ## Completion checklist - [ ] predictors are known at prediction time; - [ ] a baseline is reported; - [ ] RMSE, MAE, and R² are reported; - [ ] predictors are standardised before regularising; - [ ] penalty $\alpha$ and mixture are tuned by cross-validation; - [ ] selected predictors are not described as causes; - [ ] the test set is used once. --- ## Misconceptions to leave behind (Part 1) | Misconception | Better mental model | |---|---| | more predictors always help | each is another chance to fit noise | | the lasso's predictors are what matters | they help prediction, chosen partly by chance | --- ## Misconceptions to leave behind (Part 2) | Misconception | Better mental model | |---|---| | a low RMSE means every prediction is accurate | extremes are pulled to the average | | boosting always beats regression | only when curves and interactions exist | --- ## The chapter in one sentence > **With many predictors, shrink the coefficients or build from small trees, compare against a baseline by cross-validation, and never read a selected predictor as a cause.** --- ## Next: Chapter 14 The next chapter revisits clustering: - what counts as a group; - Gaussian mixture models and soft membership; - clusters as dense regions: DBSCAN; - evaluating a clustering; - reporting the choices behind the clusters. --- ## Questions How many predictors, and how many cases, would your model have? What is the simplest prediction your model must beat?
